detail.extracted_title: Frankincense and Celadon: How Dhofar's Ancient Ports Anchored Two Millennia of Omani-Chinese Maritime Trade
detail.excerpt: Long before modern container ships charted the Indian Ocean, the monsoon winds carried Omani stitched dhows across the South China Sea, binding the southern Arabian coast to imperial Chinese ports through aromatic resin, fine porcelain, and mutual diplomatic respect.
detail.article_html:
Walk across the limestone foundations of Al-Baleed Archaeological Park on the coast of Salalah, and the physical evidence of medieval global trade still glints beneath the soil. Alongside carved local masonry and heavy stone ship anchors, archaeologists have unearthed delicate shards of olive-green Longquan celadon, cobalt-painted Ming porcelain, and cast bronze Chinese coins pierced with square center holes. These fragments belong to an exchange spanning more than two thousand years, examined in depth by researcher Salem Ahmed Salem Al-Kathiri. Moving along the intersecting paths of the Maritime Silk Road and the Frankincense Route, sailors and merchants from Oman and China built one of pre-modern history's most enduring commercial corridors.

Pioneers of the Monsoon Sea Lanes

Historical accounts indicate that Arab mariners—with Omani navigators at the forefront—reached the southern shores of China between 203 BC and 97 AD, centuries before the rise of Islam. In 651 AD, during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan, the first official Islamic diplomatic delegation arrived at the court of the Tang Dynasty (618–907 AD). From that point onward, the port of Canton (modern-day Guangzhou) grew into a thriving base for Omani seafarers and merchants.

Among the earliest documented Omani figures to make the complete eastern voyage was the scholar and merchant Abu Ubaidah Abdullah bin Al-Qasim Al-Bahlawi, who was active around 171 AH (787 AD). Centuries later, during the eleventh century, the Omani merchant Sheikh Abdullah Al-Suhari resided in Guangzhou for years before returning home in 1072 AD, honoured by the Song imperial court with the title of "The Virtuous General." Another prominent figure of Arab-Omani lineage, recorded in Chinese chronicles as Bo-Sho-Geng (Abu Shawqi), rose to become the superintendent of merchant shipping at Guangzhou port, overseeing foreign customs and maritime commerce across the South China Sea.

Crossing between the Arabian Sea and southern China tested human endurance and astronomical skill. Omani captains departed Muscat, Sohar, Al-Baleed, or Mirbat aboard vessels constructed from coconut timber bound with coir rope, riding the northeast monsoon toward the Malabar Coast and stopping at Kalahbar on the Malay Peninsula to replenish fresh water and timber. Waiting for favourable seasonal winds at each stage meant that a single round-trip voyage between Oman and Guangzhou required more than eighteen months at sea.

Seven Grades of Sacred Dhofari Resin

At the centre of this transoceanic commerce stood a single commodity harvested from the limestone valleys behind the Dhofar mountains: Boswellia sacra frankincense. In Chinese administrative and medical treatises, Dhofari frankincense was known as Xunliu (or Xunli) and later during the Song Dynasty as Ti-ju, meaning "milk incense." Already cited in Han Dynasty (206 BC–220 AD) pharmacopoeias for relieving pain, reducing inflammation, and refreshing interior spaces, Omani frankincense became so prized by the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD) that the imperial court issued decrees placing its import under state monopoly. Archaeologists excavating Song-era underground palace tombs in Nanjing even discovered sealed caches of frankincense stored alongside royal relics.

Chinese maritime trade offices classified imported frankincense into up to seven distinct quality grades based on purity, color, and harvesting method:

  • Jian-xiang (or Di-xiang): The highest grade, consisting of round, translucent droplets collected cleanly before touching the ground.
  • Ping-ru: Resinous tears gathered immediately at the base of the trunk with minimal impurities.
  • Ping-xiang and Dai-xiang: Mid-tier grades sorted inside woven palm-leaf sacks according to size and clarity.
  • Hei-ta and Shui-shi-hei-ta: Darker resin mixed with bark or softened by moisture during the sea crossing.
  • Chan-mo: Fine frankincense dust and fragments swept from warehouse floors and burned in temple braziers.

In addition to domestic frankincense, Omani ports functioned as vital entrepôts re-exporting East African ivory, ambergris, myrrh, Socotran Dragon's Blood resin (Dam Al-Akhawayn), rosewater, pearls, and purebred Arabian horses to China. Returning west, Omani vessels filled their holds with raw silk, camphor, rhubarb, musk, ironware, agarwood, and thousands of kiln-fired ceramic vessels that graced homes and mosques along the Omani coast.

Dhofar in Chinese Imperial Chronicles and Zheng He's Fleets

The prominence of Omani ports left a clear imprint on classical Chinese geography. In his 1225 AD treatise Chu-fan-chi (Description of Foreign Peoples), the Song Dynasty customs inspector Chau Ju-Kua—a descendant of Emperor Tai-tsung—documented the geography, customs, and exports of Oman (Nu-man), Sohar (Wu-shi-wan), Dhofar (Nufa), and Mirbat (Ma-lo-ba). He noted that the people of Dhofar wore pristine white garments, abstained from wine, minted coins of gold and silver, and harvested frankincense from mountain trees scored with sharp blades during the heat of summer.

Direct maritime contact reached its zenith during the Ming Dynasty under Emperor Yongle, who commissioned the Muslim Admiral Zheng He to lead seven grand naval expeditions across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433 AD. In 1421, the ruler of Dhofar dispatched an envoy named Hadi Hassan (Hai-zai-hot-shan in Ming court annals) to Beijing bearing precious frankincense, aloes, and ostriches as diplomatic gifts. In return, subsets of Zheng He's treasure fleet anchored directly off Dhofar during both the sixth expedition (1421–1422 AD) and the seventh expedition (1431–1433 AD).

Accompanying the fleet were the Chinese Muslim chroniclers and translators Ma Huan (known as Muhammad Ma Huan, author of Ying-yai Sheng-lan) and Fei Xin (author of Hsing-ch'a Sheng-lan). Landing at Al-Baleed, Ma Huan described a peaceful stone-built coastal city where residents greeted the Chinese envoys with courtesy, traded frankincense for porcelain and silk, and conducted commerce using local gold coins called Tanjashih. Today, those written accounts and the porcelain shards resting in Dhofar's coastal soil stand as enduring proof of how Oman's maritime openness connected the Arabian Peninsula with East Asia across two thousand years.

detail.instagram_caption:
Beneath the limestone ruins of Al-Baleed Archaeological Park in Salalah, fragments of olive-green Longquan celadon, cobalt Ming porcelain, and square-holed Chinese bronze coins tell the story of an ocean corridor that lasted more than two millennia.

As documented by researcher Salem Ahmed Salem Al-Kathiri in Oman Daily, Omani sailors and merchants navigated the monsoon winds between the Arabian Sea and southern China as early as 203 BC. Known in eighth-century records through figures such as Abu Ubaidah Abdullah bin Al-Qasim Al-Bahlawi and eleventh-century merchant Sheikh Abdullah Al-Suhari, Omani seafarers endured round-trip voyages lasting over 18 months via the Malay Peninsula to reach the port of Canton (Guangzhou).

At the heart of this trade was Dhofari frankincense, recorded in Chinese pharmacopoeias as Xunliu and Ti-ju ("milk incense"). Prized by Han and Song Dynasty physicians and emperors, imported frankincense was sorted by Chinese customs authorities into seven distinct grades, while Omani dhows returned westward carrying fine porcelain, raw silk, musk, and agarwood.

During the fifteenth century, Ming Dynasty Admiral Zheng He's treasure fleets anchored off Dhofar during both his sixth (1421–1422 AD) and seventh (1431–1433 AD) voyages, recorded firsthand by Muslim chroniclers Ma Huan and Fei Xin.
